chapters.title: From Recipe to Cake
chapters.scope: Start from zero: what a program is (exact instructions a computer follows), source code vs machine code, compiled vs interpreted languages, and how C++ becomes a running program through the build pipeline (preprocess, compile, link) producing object files and finally an executable; compile time vs run time; why C++ is fast and why it is unforgiving; one language, many compilers (g++ and clang) and the idea of language standards (C++23 is the current ISO standard, C++26 finished by the committee but not yet approved by ISO); 'undefined' explained in one sentence. Then the toolchain: what a terminal is (cd, ls), a first program hello.cpp shown whole and treated as a black box (anatomy is next chapter), the compile command g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -g hello.cpp -o hello, running ./hello, the default a.out when -o is missing, choosing a standard flag (both compilers here default to C++17, so __cplusplus prints 201703 without -std; with -std=c++23 g++ 13 reports a provisional 202100 while clang 18 reports 202302), warnings flags, Debug vs Release (-g vs -O2), editors and IDEs, Compiler Explorer as a stand-in because C++ has no standard REPL, and exit status read with echo $? (return 3; gives 3). Reading the first errors, in plain words: running the source file gives bash's ./hello.cpp: Permission denied; forgetting ./ gives hello: command not found; a file with no main gives undefined reference to 'main' then collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status (the linker, not the compiler, is talking); asking g++ 13 for C++26 gives g++: error: unrecognized command-line option '-std=c++2c'; did you mean '-std=c++20'?. Classic mistakes: editing the .cpp but running the old binary (no message, old output), and believing a successful compile means a correct program.
chapters.not_yet: Line-by-line anatomy of hello.cpp (#include, main, std::cout, <<, semicolons) and the full file:line:col error anatomy belong to ch2; variables and types (ch3); multiple files, headers and how the linker joins them in depth (ch10); CMake (ch17).
chapters.visuals: Bakery pipeline picture: recipe card (.cpp) to chef (compiler) to trays (object files) to packer (linker) boxing a cake (executable), with a sign 'you cannot eat the recipe card'. Map/statechart of the build: preprocess, compile, link, run, with error roads (compiler error, linker error, Permission denied, command not found) checked against real captures. Workshop-bench machine: the compiler as a machine with dials (flags), -Wall drawn as a smoke alarm, -g as labels on every part. Walker over the terminal session: compile, ls shows the new file, run, echo $?.

The 'old binary' mistake needs a two-step capture (edit then run without recompiling).

chapters.title: Hello, Detective!
chapters.scope: Anatomy of Hello, World line by line: #include <iostream>, int main(), braces and blocks, statements end with semicolons, std::cout and the std:: prefix, << chaining, string literals in double quotes, '\n' vs std::endl (endl also flushes; prefer '\n'), comments // and /* */, whitespace and indentation freedom, return 0; and the implicit return from main, escape sequences \" \\ \t. Then reading compiler messages like a detective: the anatomy file:line:col: error: message, the optional 'In function' header line, the source excerpt with its line-number margin and caret, fix-it hints and 'did you mean' suggestions, note: lines (often pointing into /usr/include/c++/13/...), errors vs warnings (warnings end with the flag in brackets), compiler errors vs linker errors, fix the first error first because one typo cascades, warning flags -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion and -Werror, searching a message online. Real mistakes in teaching order: missing ; gives error: expected ';' before 'return' (clang: expected ';' after expression) with a fix-it caret; missing } gives error: expected '}' at end of input plus note: to match this '{'; forgetting std:: gives 'cout' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'std::cout'?; a misspelled header gives fatal error: iostrem: No such file or directory; single quotes around text give warning: character constant too long for its type; ignoring warnings (preview: warning: 'x' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]); reading the last error instead of the first; mistaking undefined reference to 'add(int, int)' for a compile error; assuming g++ catches int x = 3.7; (silent with -Wall -Wextra; only -Wconversion reports conversion from 'double' to 'int' changes value from '3.7000000000000002e+0' to '3' [-Wfloat-conversion], while clang warns by default [-Wliteral-conversion]). Show g++ and clang side by side for at least one error.
chapters.not_yet: Variables, initialisation and why uninitialised reads are dangerous (ch3; only the warning text may appear here as an example); type conversion and narrowing rules (ch4); std::format (ch5); multi-file linker errors in depth (ch10).
chapters.visuals: Conveyor-belt machine: std::cout as a belt to the screen, each << drops a box, '\n' is the 'new line' box and std::endl is that box plus 'ship the belt now'. Walker stepping hello.cpp with the screen growing. Detective's report extension or annotated panel: address (file:line:col), accusation (error), evidence (caret), witness statements (notes), checked against real captured stderr. Map of a cascade: one missing brace producing several errors, with the 'question the first suspect first' road.

chapters.title: Boxes and Odometers
chapters.scope: Variables: objects live in memory, declaring a variable with the type before the name, brace initialisation int x{5};, copy initialisation with =, value initialisation int x{}; (gives 0), initialisation vs assignment, uninitialised variables hold an indeterminate value (reading one is undefined behaviour), identifiers and naming rules, keywords, case sensitivity, const, a constexpr preview, one variable per line, declare near first use (Core Guidelines ES.20 always initialise, ES.23 prefer {}, Con.1 const by default). Mistakes: using before declaring gives 'x' was not declared in this scope; declaring twice gives error: redeclaration of 'int x'; changing a const gives error: assignment of read-only variable 'x'; reading an uninitialised int gives warning: 'x' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized] and the program's output cannot be trusted (it varies by run, optimisation level and compiler). Numbers and arithmetic: fundamental types int, double, bool, char, sizeof (sizes 'on this machine'), integer division and %, negative division truncates toward zero (7 / 2 is 3, -7 / 2 is -3, -7 % 3 is -1), precedence and parentheses, compound assignment +=, ++ and --, literals (1'000'000, 3.0, 1e3, 'A'), <cmath> std::pow and std::sqrt, ^ is not power, char prints as a letter (char c = 65; prints A; +c prints 65), floating point is approximate (0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.3 by default and 0.30000000000000004 at precision 17), integer overflow is undefined behaviour (INT_MAX + 1 shown only through UBSan: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'), integer divide by zero is undefined (shown only through UBSan's division-by-zero report), auto first look. Mistakes: average computed as sum / count with ints; choosing int vs double for a price, count or temperature.
chapters.not_yet: Keyboard input (ch4); conversions, static_cast and brace narrowing errors (ch4); the full UB and sanitizer story (ch11: here only a brief 'night-vision goggles' teaser beside each sanitizer report); fixed-width integer types, unsigned wraparound and IEEE details (ch20); std::format precision specs (ch5 first look, ch18 in depth) - use std::cout << std::setprecision(17) for the 0.1 + 0.2 demo.

chapters.not_yet: Authoring modules (toolchain support not available here); ABI and shared-library versioning (beyond this book); CMake was taught in ch17 and may be reused to drive library builds.
chapters.visuals: City with neighbourhoods: internal linkage is a street name only used locally; external linkage is a city-wide address that must be unique. Map of a build with several translation units, a static library and a shared library, with roads to multiple-definition and undefined-reference failures, each checked against captures. Machine showing the mangler: a C++ signature in, a mangled symbol out (from real nm output), and c++filt reversing it.
chapters.cast: Wren the mechanic (guide, assets/CAST.md); Linker (starring role, now a city planner); Compiler; Professor (preprocessor history).
chapters.capture_notes: Standard capture: g++ 13.3 -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g (primary, shown on pages), clang 18 -std=c++23 as secondary comparison; LC_ALL=C and -fdiagnostics-color=never so quotes are straight; compile from the program folder with relative paths; record exit codes (134/136/139), not shell words. Output via iostream and std::format only (<print> does not exist here). Needs the multi-step build recipe: compile named .o files, ar rcs for static libraries, -shared -fPIC for shared ones, and run the result with LD_LIBRARY_PATH or an rpath set by the tool. nm and c++filt outputs are deterministic for object files but list addresses and compiler-generated symbols: filter to the symbols discussed. g++ -E preprocessor output is huge: capture only small headers or filter. Capture the import std failures from both compilers as real errors.

chapters.title: Many Cooks, One Stopwatch
chapters.scope: Concurrency basics: threads and why (cores), std::thread vs std::jthread (C++20, joins automatically), joining, data races and why they are undefined behaviour, std::mutex, std::lock_guard/std::scoped_lock, std::atomic for counters, std::condition_variable as a first look, tasks with std::async and std::future, ThreadSanitizer, deadlock basics (CP.1-CP.9, CP.20, CP.25, CP.26). Mistakes: a racy counter that should reach 400000 gave different totals on different runs; TSan reports WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race; a std::thread destroyed unjoined gives terminate called without an active exception, exit 134. Performance and measurement: measure first (<chrono> steady_clock, duration_cast), Debug vs Release (-O0 vs -O2), avoiding needless copies (const&, moves), reserve, contiguous memory and caches (why vector beats list), algorithmic complexity first, the std::endl flush cost, small-string optimisation awareness, profiler awareness (gprof here; perf is not installed), looking at what the compiler did (g++ -S assembly or Compiler Explorer) (Per.1-Per.7). Mistakes: benchmarking a -O0 build; timing output differs on every run; passing big vectors by value in a hot loop; using std::endl in a million-line loop; a copy hidden in a range-for.
chapters.not_yet: Memory model and atomic orderings, lock-free structures, coroutines, parallel STL and SIMD (beyond this book).
chapters.visuals: Several cooks sharing one notebook to tally orders: without a pen-passing rule (mutex) two cooks write over each other and orders vanish. Timeline/swimlane extension showing two threads interleaving on a counter (drawn as an illustration, not as captured output), plus the fixed versions with atomic and mutex. Relay race timed with a stopwatch: you only know which runner is slow after timing each leg. Choice and predict exercises built on deterministic facts (final totals of correct programs, which build flags), never on timings.

chapters.capture_notes: Standard capture: g++ 13.3 -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g (primary, shown on pages), clang 18 -std=c++23 as secondary comparison; LC_ALL=C and -fdiagnostics-color=never so quotes are straight; compile from the program folder with relative paths; record exit codes (134/136/139), not shell words. Output via iostream and std::format only (<print> does not exist here). OWNER DECISION NEEDED: a data race is undefined behaviour, and the book rule allows UB only through g++ -fsanitize=address,undefined reports, which cannot detect races. Either approve a g++ -fsanitize=thread capture (TSan alone; it cannot combine with ASan) as a one-chapter exception, or teach the race with the illustration only and capture just the correct atomic and mutex versions (deterministic final total 400000). Interleaved output from threads must be avoided (join, then print) or marked .nondet. The unjoined-thread terminate is a normal capture (exit 134). All timing output is nondeterministic: mark every timing program .nondet, never use timings as answers, and describe speedups in words; -O0 vs -O2 needs per-program flag sidecars. gprof needs -pg and writes gmon.out into the working directory (scratch location). g++ -S assembly output is deterministic for a fixed source and flags, so it can be captured instead of Compiler Explorer.
